justification: This article is stronger on the design/illustration axis than both comparison sources. Refactoring Guru's composition-over-inheritance page uses generic, catalog-reused UML-style diagrams (a duck/animal-style class explosion) that are not tailored to one running example, gestures at the N x M subclass-explosion problem abstractly without ever showing a concrete runtime bug, and shows abbreviated/pseudocode snippets rather than full compiled programs with real output; it has no exercises. Microsoft's own OOP/inheritance guidance is text-first, has few or no diagrams, and is prescriptive rather than narrative. This article's two SVG figures are purpose-built around the single Wyvern scenario (the blocked-diamond 'before' with a clearly marked CS1721-rejected node and a duplicated-fix node, and the 'after' composition structure with the shared Flying instance visually highlighted in the accent color and outlined a second time in the enemy-pairing table), every one of its 13 code blocks is a complete program with a real, verified output panel or a red does-not-compile/throws badge, and it demonstrates an actual consequence of the anti-pattern (the Wyvern gas-damage bug, shown running and producing a wrong number) rather than just asserting the anti-pattern is bad. Three progressively harder exercises (predict-a-cast, extend-without-touching, count-the-classes) stay correctly collapsed behind <details> in every screenshot checked, including the one this article is explicit about not spoiling (the predict-the-output cast exercise). Heading hierarchy is clean (one H1, five H2 sections, no skipped levels), prose/code/diagram/exercise rhythm has no walls of text, and the :::dotnet (purple) and :::pitfall (red) callouts render as clearly distinct, theme-correct blocks in both desktop-dark and mobile-light as well as the primary light/dark pairs. Real Lighthouse is 97/100/100/100, zero console errors, zero broken links (including the cross-link to the published four-pillars-of-oop article's Collector(IPaymentGateway) example at its #how-is-abstraction-different-from-encapsulation anchor -- verified that heading and code sample exist there and the article is published, draft: false), and mobileOverflowPx is 0. It falls short of 8.5 for one concrete, binding-rule violation: the .NET exception-hierarchy output panel (the article's one piece of evidence that catching ArgumentException transparently catches two different concrete subtypes) exceeds the ~40-column mobile window and cuts off the exact tokens -- 'ArgumentNullException' and 'ArgumentOutOfRangeException' -- that the surrounding prose depends on, in both mobile-dark and mobile-light. Every other output panel and code block in the article respects the 40-column rule; this is an isolated but direct hit on WRITER_GUIDE.md's explicit rule that 'if the last column is the evidence for a claim, it must not be the one that is cut off.' A one-line reformat fixes it.
